generatedProse.concept-context: A presentation that delivers well in the School of Sport has a structure the audience can follow: an introduction that frames the question or task, a main body that develops the argument in order, and a conclusion that leaves one clear message. In sport coaching, that might mean framing a problem in a session, working through what the observation and evidence show, and closing on one recommendation. Visual aids support that structure rather than replace it. A single clear clip or diagram lands faster than a paragraph of text, but a slide crammed with detail splits the audience between you and the screen. The slides prompt; you deliver.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students present the same analysis of a training session, with the same findings to share.

Tom builds the slides first and lets them set the order. Each slide is full of text and drill detail, and the talk becomes a reading of the screen. The talk has no clear opening or close, so the group is unsure what the main coaching point is, and the slides pull their eyes away from Tom rather than supporting the argument. The material is all there, but it does not land.

Amara plans the structure first: an introduction that frames the coaching problem, a main body of three ordered points, and a conclusion with one clear recommendation for the session. Only then do the slides follow, each one a prompt or a single clear clip. The group can follow the argument, and the visual aids help it along. The delivery feels in control.

Both had the same findings. Only Amara let a structure lead and made the visual aids serve it.
generatedProse.summary: A presentation in the School of Sport delivers well when a clear structure leads it and the visual aids serve that structure. An introduction, an ordered main body and a conclusion give the audience a path through your argument, and slides that prompt rather than script keep their attention on you. You can now build a supporting structure and design visual aids that back your point. The final lesson looks at the errors that undo good preparation.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara's visual aids work better than Tom's?

items.text: They supported each point as prompts or a single clear clip, rather than carrying dense text.
They used brighter colours and more animation.
There were more slides, so the audience saw more.
They were written out in full so she could read them aloud.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara's visual aids supported each point as prompts or a clear clip, rather than carrying the talk.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the visual aids were doing, not how they looked.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's visual aids worked because they prompted and supported each point. Colour, more slides or full text are not what made them effective.
